title: "Class 17: Convergence Rates"
subtitle: "How fast the error goes away, and how we measure it"
format:
  html:
    page-layout: full

We have built a finite element solver and we have looked at its solution and its derivative.
The obvious next question is whether the answer is any good, and that question has a
surprisingly precise answer: not *what* the error is, but *how fast it goes away* as we
refine the mesh.

## What we measure the error in

The error is a function, not a number:

$$ e(x) := u(x) - u^h(x) . $$

To get a number out of it we need a norm, and we need one that can ask about derivatives,
because we already know the derivative is approximated particularly poorly. 
The **Sobolev norms** do exactly that. In one dimension:

$$
\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, dx, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \left(e_{,x}\right)^2 dx, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \left(e_{,x}\right)^2 + \left(e_{,xx}\right)^2 dx .
$$

Each one includes everything the previous one had, plus one more derivative. $H^0$ is the
same thing as $L^2$ — it only asks whether the *values* are close. $H^1$ also asks whether
the *slopes* are close. $H^2$ also asks about curvature.

In several dimensions the same thing, written with the gradient:

$$
\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \nabla e \cdot \nabla e \; d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + \nabla e \cdot \nabla e + \nabla^2 e : \nabla^2 e \; d\Omega ,
$$

or in index notation, which is often easier to implement from:

$$
\|e\|_{H^0}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 \, d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^1}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + e_{,i}\,e_{,i} \; d\Omega, \qquad
\|e\|_{H^2}^2 = \int_\Omega e^2 + e_{,i}\,e_{,i} + e_{,ij}\,e_{,ij} \; d\Omega .
$$

Repeated indices are summed, so $e_{,i}e_{,i}$ in two dimensions is
$\left(e_{,x}\right)^2 + \left(e_{,y}\right)^2$, which is exactly $\nabla e \cdot \nabla e$.

In practice we almost always report $H^0$ and $H^1$. 
$H^0$ tells you whether the solution is right, while $H^1$ tells you whether the fluxes and strains you extract from it are right, and those are usually the quantities of interest.
$H^2$ is not particularly usefule for the Poisson equation, but plays a bigger role in beam and shell problems and in mixing theory.

## What $h$ means

Every element has a size. The one the estimate uses is the **diameter** of the element ---
the longest distance between any two of its points --- and then $h$ is the largest of those
over the whole mesh:

$$ h_K = \mathrm{diam}\left(\Omega^K\right) = \max_{\underline{a},\underline{b}\,\in\,\Omega^K} \left|\underline{a}-\underline{b}\right| ,
\qquad h = \max_K h_K . $$

In one dimension that is just the length of the interval. In two and three dimensions it is
a diagonal, not an edge --- which matters, because a long thin element has a much larger
diameter than its short edge suggests.

### Quasi-uniformity is a property of a *family* of meshes

The estimates come with a hidden assumption, and it is easy to state imprecisely. A family
of meshes $\{\mathcal{T}_h\}$, indexed by $h \to 0$, is **quasi-uniform** if there is a
constant $\rho > 0$ that does **not depend on $h$** such that

$$ \min_K h_K \;\geq\; \rho \, h \qquad \text{for every mesh in the family.} $$

The whole content is in *does not depend on $h$*. Any single mesh has finitely many
elements, so $h/h_{\min}$ is automatically some finite number --- you can always find a
constant that works. **You cannot look at one mesh and say whether it is quasi-uniform.**
The question is whether that ratio stays bounded as you refine, or grows without limit.

```{=html}
<div class="cv"><svg id="qusvg" viewBox="0 0 880 230" role="img"
  aria-label="Two refinement families: uniform and graded"></svg>
<div class="cap"><b>You have to watch a sequence, not a mesh.</b> Top: uniform refinement, where
the ratio of largest to smallest element stays at 1 forever. Bottom: graded refinement toward
the left end, where the ratio grows at every level and is unbounded over the family. The
bottom family is <i>not</i> quasi-uniform.
The particular error estimators given here assume a quasi-uniform refinement, but we will see that in some cases not having such a quasi-uniform refinement may be good.
This goes to show that these a-priori error estimators are just one resource that we have to improve accuracy.
</div></div>

<script>
(function(){
var S='',INK='#18202b',GREY='#6b7684',ACC='#b8322a',OK='#1d7a4c';
function row(y,label,gen,col){
  S+='<text x="12" y="'+(y-26)+'" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="'+INK+'">'+label+'</text>';
  [0,1,2].forEach(function(lv){
    var L=150+lv*245, W=195, edges=gen(lv);
    S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+y+'" x2="'+(L+W)+'" y2="'+y+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.3"/>';
    var big=0,small=1e9;
    edges.forEach(function(t,i){ var x=L+W*t;
      S+='<line x1="'+x+'" y1="'+(y-8)+'" x2="'+x+'" y2="'+(y+8)+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.2"/>';
      if(i>0){var w=t-edges[i-1]; if(w>big)big=w; if(w<small)small=w;} });
    S+='<text x="'+(L+W/2)+'" y="'+(y+26)+'" font-size="11.5" fill="'+col+'" text-anchor="middle">h/h'+
       '<tspan baseline-shift="sub" font-size="8">min</tspan> = '+(big/small).toFixed(0)+'</text>';
  });
}
row(58,'uniform refinement', function(lv){ var n=4*Math.pow(2,lv),a=[];
  for(var i=0;i<=n;i++)a.push(i/n); return a; }, OK);
row(160,'graded toward the left', function(lv){ var n=4*Math.pow(2,lv),a=[];
  for(var i=0;i<=n;i++)a.push(Math.pow(i/n,2.5)); return a; }, ACC);
document.getElementById('qusvg').innerHTML=S;
})();
</script>
```

So why does the assumption appear at all? Because it is what lets us write the estimate in
terms of a *single* number $h$. The underlying approximation results are local --- they hold
element by element in terms of $h_K$, and need only **shape regularity**, a bound on how
stretched any individual element may be. Quasi-uniformity is the extra condition that lets
us replace every $h_K$ by one global $h$ and still have a sharp statement. 
The error constant $C$ that we will see later
degrades as $h/h_{\min}$ grows.

### Refining in the right place beats refining everywhere

A non-quasi-uniform family for mesh refinement is not always bad.
 If the solution is
hard to resolve in one small region, putting your elements there is far more effective than
spreading them evenly --- and the a-priori estimate below, written for a single $h$, simply
does not describe what you get.

Here is the demonstration. Take

$$ u(x) = \tanh\!\big(25(x-\tfrac{1}{2})\big), \qquad f = -u_{,xx} , $$

which is perfectly **smooth** --- it has derivatives of every order --- but swings from
$-1$ to $1$ across a narrow layer in the middle and is nearly flat everywhere else. Use
quadratic elements, $k=2$. Refine three ways, always to the same number of elements.

```{=html}
<div class="cv"><svg id="rfsvg" viewBox="0 0 880 350" role="img"
  aria-label="The solution, and three refinement strategies on the same domain"></svg>
<div class="cap"><b>Why that region and not another.</b> The top panel is the exact solution.
Almost all of its variation happens inside the
shaded strip &mdash; outside it, <i>u</i> is within a hair of &plusmn;1 and a single element
would reproduce it almost exactly. The three meshes below put the same sixteen elements in
different places. Only the second one puts them where the function is actually doing
something.</div></div>

<script>
(function(){
var S='',INK='#18202b',GREY='#6b7684',ACC='#b8322a',OK='#1d7a4c',BLUE='#2b5fa8',FAINT='#dfe4ea';
var K=25,C=0.5, L=250,R=840;
function u(x){ return Math.tanh(K*(x-C)); }

// ---- shaded layer strip, spanning the whole figure ----
var sx0=L+(R-L)*0.40, sx1=L+(R-L)*0.60;
S+='<rect x="'+sx0+'" y="14" width="'+(sx1-sx0)+'" height="310" fill="'+ACC+'" opacity=".06"/>';
S+='<text x="'+((sx0+sx1)/2)+'" y="12" font-size="11" fill="'+ACC+'" text-anchor="middle">the layer</text>';

// ---- solution panel ----
var y0=26,y1=150, mid=(y0+y1)/2, amp=(y1-y0)/2-10;
S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+mid+'" x2="'+R+'" y2="'+mid+'" stroke="'+FAINT+'" stroke-width="1"/>';
var d='';
for(var i=0;i<=600;i++){ var x=i/600, px=L+(R-L)*x;
  d+=(i?' L':'M')+px.toFixed(1)+' '+(mid-amp*u(x)).toFixed(1);
}
S+='<path d="'+d+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none"/>';
S+='<text x="'+(L+6)+'" y="'+(y0+12)+'" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="'+INK+'">u(x) = tanh(25(x − ½))</text>';
S+='<text x="'+(L-8)+'" y="'+(mid-amp+4)+'" font-size="11" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="end">+1</text>';
S+='<text x="'+(L-8)+'" y="'+(mid+amp+4)+'" font-size="11" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="end">−1</text>';

// ---- the three meshes ----
function row(y,label,f,col,note){
  var N=16;
  S+='<text x="12" y="'+(y+4)+'" font-size="12.5" font-weight="600" fill="'+INK+'">'+label+'</text>';
  S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+y+'" x2="'+R+'" y2="'+y+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.3"/>';
  for(var i=0;i<=N;i++){ var x=L+(R-L)*f(i/N);
    S+='<line x1="'+x+'" y1="'+(y-9)+'" x2="'+x+'" y2="'+(y+9)+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.1"/>'; }
  S+='<text x="'+R+'" y="'+(y+25)+'" font-size="11.5" fill="'+col+'" text-anchor="end">'+note+'</text>';
}
function pw(g){ return function(t){ var z=2*t-1; return 0.5+0.5*(z<0?-1:1)*Math.pow(Math.abs(z),g); }; }
row(192,'uniform',                 function(t){return t;}, BLUE,'L² rate 2.60');
row(248,'clustered at the layer',  pw(2.5),                OK,  'L² rate 2.91  —  the full degree-2 rate');
row(304,'clustered at the ends',   pw(1/2.5),              ACC, 'L² rate 0.87  —  far worse than uniform');
document.getElementById('rfsvg').innerHTML=S;
})();
</script>
```

| elements | uniform $\|e\|_{L^2}$ | at the layer | at the ends |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8   | 3.01e−2 | 7.04e−3 | 1.41e−1 |
| 16  | 1.99e−3 | 1.20e−3 | 9.54e−2 |
| 32  | 8.37e−4 | 1.49e−4 | 5.80e−2 |
| 64  | 1.18e−4 | 1.88e−5 | 3.01e−2 |
| 128 | 1.49e−5 | **2.36e−6** | 1.23e−2 |
| **observed rate** | **2.60** | **2.91** | **0.87** |

Three things to take from this.

**This has nothing to do with smoothness.** $\tanh$ is infinitely differentiable, so the
solution is as regular as anyone could ask. The only thing that differs between the three
rows is *where the elements sit*. Resolution and regularity are separate issues, and this is
the resolution one.

**Refining where it matters gives the least amount of error.** Clustering at the layer reaches 2.91 --- essentially the
rate quadratic elements are capable of --- and at 128 elements it is **six times more
accurate** than uniform for exactly the same cost. That family is deliberately not
quasi-uniform.

**Refining in the wrong place doesn't help.** Clustering at the ends means that you don't refine in the one region
that needed elements. Its measured rate is 0.87, and at 128 elements it is still *a thousand
times* less accurate than clustering at the layer. Putting elements somewhere is not the
same as putting them somewhere useful.

Note also that the uniform row reads 2.60 rather than 3. The estimate is asymptotic, and on
these meshes the layer is still only a few elements wide, so we are not yet in the range
where it applies. That is a different effect again, and we return to it later.

So when we write $\|e\| \leq C h^\beta \|u\|$ in the next section and talk about measuring a
slope, understand what it describes: **uniform refinement of a quasi-uniform family.** That
is the setting where a single $h$ means something. Adaptive and graded meshes are common and are frequently better.
Deciding where to put the elements needs different tools, a-posteriori
estimators, which we are not covering here.

## A-priori error estimates

**A priori** means *before the fact*: before you solve anything, you can say how the error
will behave, purely from the polynomial degree, the mesh size, and how smooth the exact
solution is. You do not need the computed answer to write it down. (The contrast is an
**a-posteriori** estimate, which is computed *after* you solve, out of the solution you got,
and which can give you an actual number and tell you which elements to refine. We are not
doing those here.)

The standard a-priori estimate, for a sufficiently smooth exact solution, is

$$
\boxed{\;\|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \;\leq\; C \, h^{\beta} \, \|u\|_{H^{k+1}(\Omega)},
\qquad \beta = \min\big(k+1-s,\; 2(k+1-m)\big)\;}
$$

with $k$ the polynomial degree, $s$ the norm we measure in, and $m$ the number of
derivatives on a single term of the weak form. 
For the problems we solve in this class, $m=1$, and the
second argument is never lower, so in practice

$$ \beta = k + 1 - s . $$

### When the solution is not smooth enough

If you look at the right hand side of the above boxed equation carefully, you will see that it contains $\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}$. 
The estimate is only meaningful if that quantity is **finite** --- that is, if the exact solution actually
lives in $H^{k+1}(\Omega)$. If it does not, the bound is vacuous as written, and the correct
statement replaces $k+1$ by however much regularity the solution really has.

If $u \in H^{r}(\Omega)$ and $r < k+1$, then

$$
\boxed{\;\|e\|_{H^s(\Omega)} \;\leq\; C \, h^{\min(k+1,\,r)-s} \, \|u\|_{H^{r}(\Omega)}\;}
$$

so **the rate is governed by the solution, not by the degree**, and the norm bounding it is
the one the solution actually belongs to. Once $r$ drops below $k+1$, using higher more polynomial
degree does not improve the a priori error estimate because $\min(k+1,r)$ stops moving.

This is not the $\min$ in the earlier formula doing something. That one compares the
approximation space against the variational form, and both of its arguments grow with $k$.
This is a third, separate limiter sitting outside that estimate entirely.

A worked example: suppose the exact solution happens to lie in $H^{2}$, and we
discretise it with quadratic elements, $k=2$. Then $\min(k+1, r) = \min(3, 2) = 2$, so

$$ \|e\|_{L^2} \leq C\,h^{2}\|u\|_{H^2}, \qquad \|e\|_{H^1} \leq C\,h^{1}\|u\|_{H^2} , $$

rather than the $h^3$ and $h^2$ that quadratic elements deliver on a smooth solution. One
order has been lost in each norm, and switching to cubic elements would not recover it ---
$\min(4,2)$ is still 2.

It is worth being clear in
advance that it is a *different* mechanism from anything in Section&nbsp;2.2: there, the
solution was perfectly smooth and only the mesh was badly placed. Here the mesh may be
flawless and the solution itself is the limit.

### What the constant is

The constant in this above error estimate, $C,$ is typically nebulous. 
While we don't know exactly what it is, we do know that it is **independent of**:

- the mesh size $h$, so we can talk about the rate of error decrease, and
- the exact solution $u$, because the complexity of the error in from the solution has been factored into $\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}$.

It **depends on**: the domain $\Omega$, the polynomial degree $k$, the shape-regularity and
quasi-uniformity constants of the mesh family, and the coefficients of the problem (for us,
$\underline{\underline{\kappa}}$, through how strongly elliptic the operator is).

So the estimate tells you the *slope* of the error curve and not its *height*. You cannot
use it to predict that your error will be $10^{-4}$. You can use it to predict that halving
$h$ will divide the error by $2^\beta$, and doing this in code tells you if your software is correct.

## Turning the estimate into a straight line

The estimate is a power law, which is awkward to look at. Take a logarithm of both sides:

$$
\log \|e\|_{H^s} \;\leq\; \log\left(C\,\|u\|_{H^{k+1}}\right) + \beta \log h .
$$

Everything in the first term on the right is a constant — it does not change as we refine.
So if we plot $\log\|e\|$ against $\log h$, we should see a **straight line of slope
$\beta$**, sitting at a height we do not get to predict:

$$ \underbrace{\log\|e\|}_{y} = \beta \underbrace{\log h}_{x} + \underbrace{\log(C\|u\|)}_{\text{intercept}} . $$

Consequently, convergence results typically always shown on log–log axes. The quantity we care
about is a slope, and only these axes make it a slope.

### Dyadic refinement

To measure that slope we typically refine the mesh **dyadically**, where each level halves the element
size, so $h_{i+1} = h_i/2$. In one dimension that means splitting every element in two; in
two dimensions, splitting every element into four.

```{=html}
<div class="cv"><svg id="dysvg" viewBox="0 0 880 300" role="img"
  aria-label="Dyadic refinement in one and two dimensions"></svg>
<div class="cap"><b>Each level halves <i>h</i>.</b> In 1D the element count doubles; in 2D it
quadruples, because each element splits in both directions. The element <i>size</i> halves
either way, which is what the estimate is written in terms of. Note what this costs: in 2D,
three levels of refinement is 64 times as many elements.</div></div>

<script>
(function(){
var S='',INK='#18202b',GREY='#6b7684',FAINT='#dfe4ea',BLUE='#2b5fa8';
// 1D row
S+='<text x="12" y="40" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="'+INK+'">one dimension</text>';
[2,4,8].forEach(function(n,r){
  var L=150+r*250, W=200, y=36;
  S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+y+'" x2="'+(L+W)+'" y2="'+y+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.4"/>';
  for(var i=0;i<=n;i++){ var x=L+W*i/n;
    S+='<line x1="'+x+'" y1="'+(y-8)+'" x2="'+x+'" y2="'+(y+8)+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.3"/>'; }
  S+='<text x="'+(L+W/2)+'" y="'+(y+28)+'" font-size="11.5" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="middle">'+
     n+' elements, h = 1/'+n+'</text>';
});
// 2D row
S+='<text x="12" y="130" font-size="13" font-weight="600" fill="'+INK+'">two dimensions</text>';
[2,4,8].forEach(function(n,r){
  var L=150+r*250, T=110, W=150;
  for(var i=0;i<=n;i++){ var t=L+W*i/n, v=T+W*i/n;
    S+='<line x1="'+t+'" y1="'+T+'" x2="'+t+'" y2="'+(T+W)+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="'+(i%n===0?1.4:0.7)+'"/>';
    S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+v+'" x2="'+(L+W)+'" y2="'+v+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="'+(i%n===0?1.4:0.7)+'"/>'; }
  S+='<text x="'+(L+W/2)+'" y="'+(T+W+20)+'" font-size="11.5" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="middle">'+
     (n*n)+' elements, h = 1/'+n+'</text>';
  if(r===0){ S+='<rect x="'+L+'" y="'+T+'" width="'+(W/n)+'" height="'+(W/n)+'" fill="'+BLUE+'" opacity=".18"/>'; }
  if(r===1){ S+='<rect x="'+L+'" y="'+T+'" width="'+(W/2)+'" height="'+(W/2)+'" fill="'+BLUE+'" opacity=".18"/>'; }
});
S+='<text x="150" y="285" font-size="11.5" fill="'+BLUE+'">the shaded element splits into four</text>';
document.getElementById('dysvg').innerHTML=S;
})();
</script>
```

Because each level halves $h$, the slope between two consecutive levels has a very simple
form. Starting from

$$ \boxed{\;\beta \approx \frac{\log\|e_{i+1}\| - \log\|e_{i}\|}{\log h_{i+1} - \log h_{i}}\;} $$

and substituting $h_{i+1} = h_i/2$, the denominator is just $-\log 2$, so

$$ \beta \approx \log_2\!\left(\frac{\|e_i\|}{\|e_{i+1}\|}\right)$$

In words: **halve the mesh, and the rate is the base-2 logarithm of how many times smaller
the error got.** If the error drops by a factor of 4, the rate is 2. By 8, the rate is 3.

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
var MODE='lin';
var INK='#18202b',GREY='#6b7684',FAINT='#dfe4ea',ACC='#b8322a',BLUE='#2b5fa8',OK='#1d7a4c';
// measured with the Class 15 solver on u = sin(pi x), dyadic refinement
var DATA={
 1:{c:BLUE,L2:[1.509e-1,3.928e-2,9.921e-3,2.487e-3,6.220e-4,1.555e-4]},
 2:{c:OK  ,L2:[1.519e-2,1.952e-3,2.457e-4,3.076e-5,3.847e-6,4.809e-7]},
 3:{c:ACC ,L2:[1.388e-3,8.868e-5,5.573e-6,3.488e-7,2.181e-8,1.363e-9]}
};
var HS=[0.5,0.25,0.125,0.0625,0.03125,0.015625];

function draw(){
  var S='',L=78,R=856,T=28,B=352;
  var log = (MODE==='log');
  var xmin=log?Math.log10(HS[HS.length-1]):0, xmax=log?Math.log10(HS[0]):HS[0];
  var allv=[]; [1,2,3].forEach(function(p){ DATA[p].L2.forEach(function(v){allv.push(v);}); });
  var vmin=Math.min.apply(null,allv), vmax=Math.max.apply(null,allv);
  var ymin=log?Math.log10(vmin):0, ymax=log?Math.log10(vmax):vmax;
  function X(h){ var t=log?(Math.log10(h)-xmin)/(xmax-xmin):(h-xmin)/(xmax-xmin); return L+(R-L)*t; }
  function Y(v){ var t=log?(Math.log10(v)-ymin)/(ymax-ymin):(v-ymin)/(ymax-ymin); return B-(B-T)*t; }
  S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+B+'" x2="'+R+'" y2="'+B+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.2"/>';
  S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+T+'" x2="'+L+'" y2="'+B+'" stroke="'+INK+'" stroke-width="1.2"/>';
  // ticks
  HS.forEach(function(h){ var x=X(h);
    S+='<line x1="'+x+'" y1="'+B+'" x2="'+x+'" y2="'+(B+5)+'" stroke="'+GREY+'"/>';
    S+='<text x="'+x+'" y="'+(B+18)+'" font-size="10.5" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="middle">'+
       (log?('1/'+Math.round(1/h)):h.toFixed(3))+'</text>'; });
  if(log){ for(var e=-9;e<=0;e++){ var v=Math.pow(10,e); if(v<vmin/2||v>vmax*2) continue;
      var y=Y(v); S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+y+'" x2="'+R+'" y2="'+y+'" stroke="'+FAINT+'" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/>';
      S+='<text x="'+(L-7)+'" y="'+(y+4)+'" font-size="10.5" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="end">1e'+e+'</text>'; } }
  else { [0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1].forEach(function(f){ var v=vmax*f, y=Y(v);
      S+='<line x1="'+L+'" y1="'+y+'" x2="'+R+'" y2="'+y+'" stroke="'+FAINT+'" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/>';
      S+='<text x="'+(L-7)+'" y="'+(y+4)+'" font-size="10.5" fill="'+GREY+'" text-anchor="end">'+v.toFixed(2)+'</text>'; }); }
  [1,2,3].forEach(function(p){
    var d=DATA[p], path='';
    d.L2.forEach(function(v,i){ path+=(i?' L':'M')+X(HS[i]).toFixed(1)+' '+Y(v).toFixed(1); });
    S+='<path d="'+path+'" stroke="'+d.c+'" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none"/>';
    d.L2.forEach(function(v,i){ S+='<circle cx="'+X(HS[i]).toFixed(1)+'" cy="'+Y(v).toFixed(1)+'" r="3.2" fill="'+d.c+'"/>'; });
    var lx=X(HS[0])-10, ly=Y(d.L2[0]);
    S+='<text x="'+lx+'" y="'+(ly-9)+'" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="'+d.c+
       '" text-anchor="end">p = '+p+(log?'  (slope '+(p+1)+')':'')+'</text>';
  });
  S+='<text x="'+((L+R)/2)+'" y="388" font-size="12" fill="'+INK+'" text-anchor="middle">element size h'+(log?'   (log scale)':'')+'</text>';
  S+='<text x="18" y="'+((T+B)/2)+'" font-size="12" fill="'+INK+'" transform="rotate(-90 18 '+((T+B)/2)+')" text-anchor="middle">||e||'+(log?'  (log scale)':'')+'</text>';
  document.getElementById('cvsvg').innerHTML=S;
  document.getElementById('cvcap').innerHTML = log
   ? 'On log&ndash;log axes each degree is a <b>straight line</b>, and the slope is &beta; = k+1 = 2, 3 and 4. '
     + 'The lines sit at different heights &mdash; that is the constant C, which we do not get to predict. '
     + 'What we <i>can</i> predict, and check, is that they are straight and that their slopes are the right integers.'
   : 'On ordinary axes all three curves collapse onto the bottom of the plot almost immediately and '
     + 'become impossible to tell apart. There is no visible difference between a rate of 2 and a rate of 4. '
     + '<b>Switch to log&ndash;log</b> and the same numbers separate into three straight lines.';
  document.getElementById('cvnote').textContent =
    'measured with our 1D solver on u = sin(πx), L² error, dyadic refinement';
}
document.getElementById('cvax').addEventListener('click',function(ev){
  var b=ev.target.closest('button'); if(!b) return; MODE=b.dataset.v;
  [].forEach.call(this.querySelectorAll('button'),function(x){x.setAttribute('aria-pressed',x===b?'true':'false');});
  draw(); });
draw();
})();
</script>
```

Here are the numbers behind that plot, measured with our own solver. The rate column is
$\log_2$ of the ratio of consecutive errors:

| $h$ | $\|e\|_{L^2}$, $k{=}1$ | rate | $\|e\|_{L^2}$, $k{=}2$ | rate | $\|e\|_{L^2}$, $k{=}3$ | rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1/2  | 1.51e−1 | —    | 1.52e−2 | —    | 1.39e−3 | —    |
| 1/4  | 3.93e−2 | 1.94 | 1.95e−3 | 2.96 | 8.87e−5 | 3.97 |
| 1/8  | 9.92e−3 | 1.99 | 2.46e−4 | 2.99 | 5.57e−6 | 3.99 |
| 1/16 | 2.49e−3 | 2.00 | 3.08e−5 | 3.00 | 3.49e−7 | 4.00 |
| 1/32 | 6.22e−4 | 2.00 | 3.85e−6 | 3.00 | 2.18e−8 | 4.00 |
| 1/64 | 1.56e−4 | 2.00 | 4.81e−7 | 3.00 | 1.36e−9 | 4.00 |

Two things worth noticing. The rates approach $k+1$ from below rather than hitting it
immediately — the coarsest meshes are not yet in the range where the estimate applies. And
the measured values are clean integers, which is exactly why this is such a good test of
whether your code is right: a bug in assembly usually shows up as a rate of 1.4 or 0.9
rather than as an obviously wrong picture.

One more caution when using higher degree polynomials: The error cannot fall below what double
precision can represent, so once it reaches roughly $10^{-13}$ the curve flattens and the
measured rate collapses — not because the method stopped working or is not accurate, but because the error estimate cannot capture it. On this same problem at $k=5$, the rate holds at 6.00 out to 16
elements and then reads **4.94** at 32, where the error is already $8.6\times10^{-13}$.
If a high-degree run looks like it has stopped converging, check the size of the error
before concluding that something is broken.

## Actually computing the error norm

The norms above are integrals over $\Omega$, and we evaluate them the same way we evaluate
every other integral in this course: break the domain into elements, push each element back
to the parent domain, and apply Gaussian quadrature.

**Step 1 — split the global integral into element integrals.**

$$ \|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 = \int_\Omega \left(u - u^h\right)^2 d\Omega
= \sum_{e} \int_{\Omega^e} \left(u - u^h\right)^2 d\Omega . $$

**Step 2 — change variables to the parent domain.** Each element integral becomes an
integral over the parent element, with the Jacobian determinant accounting for the change
of area (or length):

$$ \int_{\Omega^e} \left(u - u^h\right)^2 d\Omega
= \int_{\square} \left(u\!\left(\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi})\right) - u^h(\underline{\xi})\right)^2
J^e(\underline{\xi}) \; d\square ,
\qquad J^e = \det\left(DF^e\right) . $$

**Step 3 — apply quadrature.**

$$ \boxed{\;\|e\|_{H^0(\Omega)}^2 \approx \sum_e \sum_q w_q
\left(u\!\left(\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}_q)\right) - u^h(\underline{\xi}_q)\right)^2
J^e(\underline{\xi}_q)\;} $$

For the $H^1$ norm, add the gradient term, which also uses $DF^{-T}$.

$$ \|e\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 \approx \sum_e \sum_q w_q \left[
\left(u - u^h\right)^2 +
\left(\nabla_{\underline{x}} u - DF^{-T}\nabla_{\underline{\xi}} u^h\right)\cdot
\left(\nabla_{\underline{x}} u - DF^{-T}\nabla_{\underline{\xi}} u^h\right)
\right] J^e \; . $$

### The two solutions are evaluated differently

Inside that sum there are two things being evaluated at the same quadrature point, and they
are reached by different routes.

**The approximate solution is evaluated directly in the reference domain.** It is built from
local basis functions, and the IEN array tells us which coefficients to use:

$$ u^h(\underline{\xi}_q) = \sum_{a=0}^{n_{en}-1} d_{\,\mathrm{IEN}(a,e)} \; N_a(\underline{\xi}_q) . $$

No mapping is needed. The basis functions are *defined* on the parent element, so $\xi_q$ is
already the right input.

**The exact solution must be evaluated at the physical point.** $u$ is a function of
$\underline{x}$, so we first have to find where this quadrature point actually sits in space,
using the spatial mapping:

$$ \underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}_q) = \sum_{a=0}^{n_{en}-1} \underline{x}_a \, N_a(\underline{\xi}_q),
\qquad\text{then evaluate } u\!\left(\underline{x}^e(\underline{\xi}_q)\right) . $$

This is the same two-step move you already made when assembling the local force vector,
where $f$ had to be evaluated at $\underline{x}(\underline{\xi}_q)$ rather than at
$\underline{\xi}_q$. If you mix the two up — feeding $\xi_q$ straight into $u$ — the code
runs, the error comes out finite, and the convergence rate is wrong.

### A practical warning about quadrature

The error $e = u - u^h$ is **not** a polynomial, because $u$ generally is not one. So the
quadrature rule that was exact for your stiffness matrix is *not* exact here, and if you use
too few points you end up measuring your quadrature error instead of your discretization
error. Use more points than you think you need and confirm that adding points does not change the answer.

## Where this is going

- **Class 17** works through the estimate itself, these plots, and how to interpret a
  measured slope that is not what you expected.
- **Class 18** takes up *why* the estimate is true — Galerkin orthogonality, and the fact
  that the finite element solution is the best approximation available in its space.

Two things we are deliberately leaving until later. The estimate assumes the exact solution
is smooth enough to live in $H^{k+1}$; when it is not, the rate is capped by the solution's
own roughness instead, and no amount of polynomial degree fixes it. And we have said nothing
yet about where the exact solution $u$ comes from in the first place — on a real problem you
do not have one. The answer is to **manufacture** one, and that is the first thing we will do
next class.
